The paper presents an integrated approach to the optimum design of actively controlled composite wings, combining analysis techniques from structures, aerodynamics, and control systems.

The equivalent plate structural modeling approach can represent multi-element wing-control surface configurations and generate stiffness and mass matrices using analytic integration, leading to fast computation times.

The Piecewise Continuous Kernel Function Method (PCKFM) is used for subsonic/supersonic lifting surface unsteady aerodynamics, which is faster and more accurate than the doublet lattice method, especially for configurations with control surfaces.

The Minimum State Method is used for finite state modeling of the unsteady aerodynamic forces, which can achieve a given level of approximation accuracy with a smaller increase in the order of the state-space model compared to other methods.
The paper aims to bridge the gap between overly simplified and detailed analysis techniques, and to study the construction of robust approximations to behavior functions.

The current research directions mentioned in the paper are: 1) adding control system sizing design variables to the design space, and 2) expanding the design space to include structural and aerodynamic shape design variables.
The equivalent plate modeling capability allows for more detailed modeling of control surfaces compared to previous work, as the degree of detail in modeling control surfaces is not limited.

Extensive numerical tests were carried out to study the accuracy of the equivalent plate modeling and assess its computational efficiency, with good correlation to finite element results and ground vibration test data.

A typical computation time for the static analysis of a wing, including the calculation of 384 displacement, slope, and stress constraints and their sensitivities, is 12.6 cpu seconds on an IBM 3090 computer.
The analysis and constraint generation for the YF16 wing, including six static load cases and natural modes, takes 18.9 seconds, demonstrating the computational efficiency of the approach.

The paper mentions that the first bending frequency of the cantilevered YF16 wing calculated by the present code is 6.5% below the reference ground vibration test result, and that further refinement of the model is possible.

The paper states that the quality of the correlation between the mode shapes generated by the new multi-element equivalent plate analysis and the finite element results can be attributed to the high order of control surface displacement representation and better modeling of elastic point attachment of the control surfaces to the wing box.

The paper highlights that including lifting surface modeling in the analysis is important for the synthesis of real wings, as lifting surface aerodynamics are widely accepted in the aerospace industry for flutter and gust response analysis.

The Minimum State Method for finite state modeling of unsteady aerodynamics is chosen to reduce the computational cost of control system analysis and behavior sensitivity analysis, as it can achieve a given level of approximation accuracy with a smaller increase in the order of the state-space model.

The paper mentions that the iterative process used in the Minimum State Method for determining the approximation matrices is time-consuming, and that there is relatively little experience with applying the method to real configurations.
